title: Shai Hope's Century Powers Record Chase as West Indies Level T20 Series
excerpt: An unbeaten 102 from Shai Hope dragged West Indies past 250 in Ranchi, sealing the highest successful T20I chase in their history and leveling the five-match series 1-1.
body:
• West Indies chased down India's 249/5 with nine balls to spare, winning the second T20I by six wickets at the JSCA International Stadium in Ranchi to level the five-match series 1-1.
  • Captain Shai Hope anchored the record chase with an unbeaten 102 off 45 balls, finishing it with a six off Axar Patel, while Sherfane Rutherford's 84 off 37 balls turned the game after a dropped catch on 38.
  • India's bowling let a dream start slip: Mayank Yadav struck twice in the opening over and finished with three wickets, but the dropped catch and the death overs cost the hosts a match they controlled early.
  • The series now heads to Indore for the third T20I on Sunday with everything to play for — a live series, rather than the 2-0 Indian lead that seemed certain after the first over of the chase.

Ranchi witnessed one of the great T20I chases on Friday night. West Indies, chasing India's imposing 249 for 5, got home with nine balls to spare to win the second T20I by six wickets and level the five-match series at 1-1.

Captain Shai Hope led from the front with an unbeaten 102 from 45 balls, nine sixes and six fours, sealing the win — and his century — with a six off Axar Patel in the 19th over. West Indies finished on 252 for 4 in 18.3 overs, their highest successful run chase in T20 internationals and the second-highest in men's T20I history, behind only South Africa's 259 against West Indies at Centurion in 2023.

It did not look possible after the first over. Mayank Yadav tore through West Indies' top order, removing Nicholas Pooran and Shimron Hetmyer off consecutive deliveries, then returned to dismiss Rovman Powell for 24 in the sixth over. One of his deliveries was clocked at 149.5 kph. When the visitors slipped to five for two inside the opening exchanges, India looked on course for a commanding 2-0 series lead.

Hope and Sherfane Rutherford had other ideas. Rutherford blazed 84 from 37 balls with seven sixes and seven fours, and his 120-run fourth-wicket stand with Hope — the highest fourth-wicket partnership for West Indies in T20I history, according to Sports Now — ripped the game back from India. Rutherford, dropped on 38 by Mayank Yadav at short fine leg, made the error hurt: he kept hitting until Kuldeep Yadav finally ended the stand. Romario Shepherd then applied the finish, unbeaten on 34 from 13 balls.

"But when you chase here in India, you always give yourself a chance. You always think you're in the game, regardless of what score is on the board."

— Shai Hope, West Indies Captain

Context & Background

The series had begun with an emphatic Indian statement. In the first T20I on October 7, Shreyas Iyer struck his maiden T20I hundred as India won by eight wickets — a result that suggested the gulf between the sides, with West Indies' white-ball fortunes in a prolonged slump.

https://x.com/KashmirLife/status/2108608437768905013

Ranchi was expected to follow the script. India's 249 for 5 was built on Sanju Samson's 82 from 41 balls, after he and Abhishek Sharma raced to 42 inside four overs. Ishan Kishan contributed 43, while Iyer and Tilak Varma added an 83-run stand off just 32 balls. Roston Chase was the pick of the West Indies attack, dismissing Sharma, Kishan and Shivam Dube, while Shamar Springer accounted for Samson. India's 249 for 5 was its highest T20I total against West Indies, surpassing the 244 posted in the United States in 2016.

For Hope, the knock also carried a captain's imprint. The chase demanded calm after the early carnage, and he paced it — rotating early, then opening his shoulders alongside Rutherford. "But five for two was always going to be challenging," Hope admitted. "When we got that partnership there, we just got some more impetus in the innings."

Impact & Analysis

India's defeat will sting because of how far ahead they were. Two wickets in the first over, a 149.5 kph pace spearhead in form, and a target of 250 that few sides chase down. But T20 cricket punishes one loose link, and the dropped catch at short fine leg proved decisive — Rutherford was on 38 when Mayank shelled him, and he scored 46 more runs that effectively swung the series level.

The death bowling offered no answers. Hope's nine sixes came against an attack that had nowhere to hide once the required rate settled under control. India's only wickets after the powerplay came from Kuldeep Yadav and Mayank, whose three-for ended as a footnote in a lost cause. A side that had 249 on the board and the opposition five for two cannot reasonably lose — and that is the wound this result will leave.

For West Indies, it is the kind of win that changes a tour's temperature. Chasing 250 against India, in India, after losing two wickets for nothing, is a statement their camp can carry into the rest of the series.

Diaspora Angle

India–West Indies cricket remains a marquee draw for the Indian diaspora in the United States and the Caribbean, and a record chase that keeps a five-match series alive is exactly the kind of drama that sustains that bond — the tour now heads to Indore with the contest wide open rather than already settled.

What's Next

The third T20I is in Indore on Sunday, and the series narrative has flipped. India must solve its death bowling and hold its catches; West Indies, suddenly believing, know their middle order can hunt down anything. At 1-1 with three to play, a series that threatened to drift toward a home procession is suddenly a genuine contest.
